name: Screen Blend Texture Overlay
use_when: A transition, highlight, or scene needs texture such as light leaks, dust, electricity, sparks, or subtle atmosphere.
The overlay has a black background that can become transparent with Screen/Add-style blending.
The edit needs a small premium texture without rebuilding the scene.
A stylized effect fades too early and needs a short black-backed or duplicated tail to preserve the intended visual beat.
A still-image composite needs black-background fire, glow, sparks, or atmosphere to become a believable moving element.
A screen recording should feel like it was filmed through glass or by a camera rather than captured as a flat digital screen.
avoid_when: The overlay is only decoration and has no emphasis, transition, or mood job.
The texture hides faces, captions, UI, products, or proof.
The project tone is restrained and texture would feel fake or cheap.

timeline_pattern.pattern: visual_beat -> choose_texture_overlay -> screen_blend -> trim_to_beat -> adjust_opacity_color -> check_readability -> add_sfx_if_needed
timeline_pattern.blend_rule: Use Screen/Add-style blending for black-background texture overlays and verify that black disappears cleanly.
timeline_pattern.placement_rule: When the overlay represents a real scene element such as fire, resize and position it against the source object before judging opacity or grade.
timeline_pattern.job_rule: Use overlays as highlighters, transition covers, mood texture, or impact accents, not constant noise.
timeline_pattern.range_rule: Trim overlays to the specific beat so they do not linger over the next idea.
timeline_pattern.tail_rule: If extending an effect tail, duplicate only enough layers or backing duration to finish the beat, then clear before the next focus.
timeline_pattern.filmed_screen_rule: For documentary screen recordings, use glass, glare, dust, or monitor texture as a realism layer and lower opacity until UI and source text remain readable.

motion.rule: Texture overlay motion should support the underlying beat and should not become the primary focus unless it is the intended transition.

keyframe_values.filmed_screen_opacity: For a glass texture over a screen recording, opacity around 35-40% can be a starting point; reduce if UI, cursor, captions, or source text suffer.
keyframe_values.screen_texture_blend: Color Burn can create a camera-filmed screen feel on some textures; Screen, Overlay, Soft Light, or lower opacity may be better depending on the plate.

sound.rule: Add SFX only when the texture marks a real transition or impact; avoid sound on every decorative overlay.

captions.rule: Captions and important text must remain readable through the overlay's brightest frames.

color.rule: Tint or reduce opacity so the texture fits the palette and does not create compression ugliness.

implementation.ffmpeg: Use blend modes such as screen/lighten approximations or alpha-preprocessed overlays; inspect bright frames for text collisions.
implementation.remotion: Model overlays with assetRef, blendMode, opacity, tint, startFrame, endFrame, and readabilityCheckFrames.
implementation.blender: Composite texture overlays with screen/add blending and keyframed opacity when building rendered inserts.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Place overlay above footage or a still image, set blend mode to Screen or similar, resize it to the motivated source area, trim to beat, and lower opacity. For filmed-screen texture, place a glass or monitor texture above the screen recording, try Color Burn or another blend mode, and start around 35-40% opacity before readability QC. For short effect tails, add a black backing/matte or duplicate the effect layer only until the intended beat finishes.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Place black-background or glass texture on a higher track, set blend mode to Screen/Overlay/Soft Light/Color Burn as appropriate, resize it to the motivated source area, trim it to the transition/highlight, adjust opacity or Lumetri/tint, and check captions. For effect tails, duplicate or loop the overlay inside a nest and fade it out before the next focus.

common_mistakes: Leaving texture overlays running over unrelated beats.
Using bright light leaks over captions or faces.
Adding overlays because they look fancy rather than because they highlight or transition.
Letting overlays create banding, noise, or compression dirt.
Extending an effect tail until it becomes visual clutter instead of emphasis.
Using a fire, glow, or atmosphere overlay that does not line up with a plausible source in the base image.
Making a screen recording look cinematic while hiding the UI detail or source text the viewer needs.
qc: Can the overlay's job be named?
Does the blend remove the black background cleanly?
Does the overlay start and end on the intended beat?
Are captions, faces, UI, products, and proof readable through the overlay?
Does the overlay fit the project's color and tone?
If the effect tail is extended, does it clear before the next beat and avoid muddy duplicate layers?
If the overlay represents a real source like fire, does it align with the object or region creating that light?
For filmed-screen texture, can the viewer still read UI, cursor motion, source text, and captions?
